blocks.text: Data Leakage established a genuinely important discipline, respect the real order of time and information, never let a model see anything at training time that would not genuinely be available at real prediction time. Train Validation Test Split is where that discipline stops being an abstract principle and becomes a concrete, repeatable procedure applied to every single dataset before real modeling work begins.

This topic, the last in the Data Collection and Understanding module, covers why a dataset genuinely needs to be divided into three distinct pieces rather than two, what each piece is actually used for, the typical ratios used in real practice, and the different splitting strategies, random, stratified, and time based, needed depending on what kind of data is genuinely being split.
1. Why a Dataset Genuinely Needs to Be Split at All

blocks.alt: All data splits into a train set and a test set

blocks.text: A model evaluated on the exact same data it was trained on will almost always look genuinely excellent, because it has effectively memorized the answers rather than genuinely learned a pattern that generalizes to new, unseen data. This is precisely the same danger covered as duplicate leakage in the previous topic, just at the scale of the entire dataset rather than a single duplicated row.

Splitting the data into separate pieces, some genuinely held back from training, is the only reliable way to estimate how a model will actually perform on real, new data it has genuinely never seen before, which is, after all, the entire point of building it.
2. The Three Genuine Pieces and What Each One Is For

blocks.alt: Train fits the model, validation tunes it, and test gives the final check

blocks.text: The training set is genuinely the largest piece, and the only one the model actually learns from directly, adjusting its internal parameters to fit the patterns present in this data. The validation set is held back from training and used instead to genuinely compare different models or different hyperparameter settings against each other, choosing whichever performs best on data the model did not train on.

The test set is the genuinely final, most protected piece, touched only once, after every decision about the model has already been made, to produce an honest, unbiased estimate of real world performance. Confusing the roles of these three pieces, especially using the test set the way the validation set should be used, is one of the most genuinely damaging mistakes covered later in this topic.

blocks.text: 3. Typical Ratios Used in Real Practice

blocks.alt: A common split is 70 percent train, 15 percent validation, 15 percent test

blocks.text: A genuinely common real split allocates around 70 percent of the data to training, with the remaining 30 percent split roughly evenly between validation and testing, often expressed as a 70, 15, 15 split. For genuinely very large datasets, the validation and test portions can shrink to a smaller percentage while still containing plenty of raw rows to give a reliable estimate, since what matters is having genuinely enough examples, not necessarily a fixed percentage.

For genuinely smaller datasets, a larger validation and test share is often used to make sure both are genuinely large enough to give a stable, trustworthy estimate, since a validation set with only a handful of rows can give a genuinely misleading, noisy signal about how well a model is actually doing.
4. How the Validation Set Actually Gets Used

blocks.alt: A model variant is tried, checked on validation, and the best one is picked

blocks.text: The validation set is genuinely revisited many times over the course of a real project, try a model, check how it performs on validation data, adjust a hyperparameter or try a different model entirely, check validation performance again, and repeat this cycle for as long as it keeps genuinely improving results. This iterative loop is exactly what the Hyperparameter Tuning and Cross Validation modules later in this course cover in much greater depth.

Because the validation set gets used this many times, the model, in a real sense, indirectly gets tuned to fit it, which is precisely why a completely separate, untouched test set is genuinely still needed at the end, to check performance on data that had no influence at all, not even the indirect influence coming from repeated validation checks.

blocks.title: Why this matters
blocks.content: Because a model gets indirectly shaped by every decision made using validation results, the validation set genuinely stops being a perfectly unbiased estimate of real performance after enough rounds of tuning. The test set exists specifically to give one final, genuinely unbiased answer.

blocks.text: 5. The Test Set Has Exactly One Rule

blocks.alt: The test set gets touched exactly once

blocks.text: The test set should genuinely be touched exactly once, after every single modeling decision, every hyperparameter, every choice between competing models, has already been finalized using only the training and validation sets. Checking test performance early, then going back to adjust the model based on what was seen, quietly turns the test set into a second validation set, destroying the one genuinely honest number a project has left.

This rule can feel genuinely uncomfortable in practice, since it means going into that final check without the ability to fix anything discovered there, but that discomfort is exactly the point, an evaluation that can still be gamed is not a genuinely honest evaluation at all.

blocks.title: A common, costly mistake
blocks.content: Peeking at test set performance during development, and adjusting the model in response, genuinely destroys the honesty of that number. If the test set has already been checked once, treat any further adjustment as needing a genuinely fresh test set to remain trustworthy.

blocks.text: 6. A Worked Example

Using scikit-learn, the standard Python library for this exact task, splitting a dataset into training, validation, and test sets is genuinely a two step process, since the built in function only splits into two pieces at a time.

code.content:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({
    "square_feet": range(100),
    "price": range(100),
})

# First split: 70 percent train, 30 percent held out
train_df, holdout_df = train_test_split(df, test_size=0.30, random_state=42)

# Second split: divide the holdout evenly into validation and test
val_df, test_df = train_test_split(holdout_df, test_size=0.50, random_state=42)

print(len(train_df), len(val_df), len(test_df))

blocks.text: Setting a fixed random_state genuinely matters here too, it makes the split reproducible, so rerunning the same code later produces the exact same three pieces rather than a genuinely different random split each time.
7. Three Genuine Splitting Strategies

blocks.alt: Splitting strategies include random, stratified, and time-based splits

blocks.text: A plain random split, where rows are assigned to each piece in any order, is genuinely appropriate for ordinary tabular data, the kind covered earlier in this module, where row order carries no meaning. A stratified split is a genuinely more careful variant used when a target class is imbalanced, it deliberately preserves the same proportion of each class across training, validation, and test, so a rare class does not accidentally end up missing entirely from one piece.

A time based split is genuinely required whenever the data is a time series, exactly the case covered in the Time Series Data topic and reinforced as temporal leakage in the previous topic, training must always come from an earlier period than validation and test, never chosen randomly, or the split itself creates leakage.

blocks.text: 8. Applying the Leakage Prevention Discipline Here

This topic is genuinely the concrete home of the train test contamination prevention covered in the previous topic, split the data into its three pieces first, before fitting any scaler, encoder, or other transformation. Fit every transformation using only the training set, then apply that exact same already fitted transformation to the validation and test sets, never refitting on either of them.

Following this order consistently is genuinely what keeps the validation and test numbers honest, an average, a scaling factor, or an encoding computed even partly from validation or test data would let a small amount of that data information leak backward into the training process, undermining the entire reason for splitting in the first place.
9. Closing Out Data Collection and Understanding

blocks.alt: Data Collection and Understanding is complete, Exploratory Data Analysis comes next

blocks.text: This topic closes out the Data Collection and Understanding module, which started with the basic shapes data can take, structured, unstructured, tabular, and time series, moved through where that data genuinely comes from and whether it can be trusted, and now ends with the concrete discipline of dividing a clean dataset into training, validation, and test sets the right way.

With a properly split, leakage free dataset now in hand, the natural next step is to actually get to know it in detail, which is exactly what the Exploratory Data Analysis module that follows takes on, examining distributions, relationships, and patterns inside the training data specifically, never peeking at the test set along the way.

items: Splitting a dataset is necessary to genuinely estimate how a model performs on new, unseen data.
Training, validation, and test sets each serve a genuinely distinct, separate role.
A common real ratio is around 70 percent train, 15 percent validation, 15 percent test.
The validation set is used repeatedly for tuning; the test set is genuinely touched only once, at the end.
Random splits suit ordinary tabular data, stratified splits preserve class balance, time based splits are required for time series.
Split before fitting any transformation, and fit transformations only on the training set, exactly as the previous topic on leakage requires.
